clue.text: Still cracking a number of the middle bones?

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one word gets put inside the other

parts.note: the median is the middle value in an ordered set of numbers
still and calm are synonyms

explanation.surface: Something motionless breaking the small bones in the middle of the body, as if describing an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bones' is the nickname of the ship's doctor in Star Trek, and 'sawbones' is slang for a surgeon; the question mark flags that informal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Bones is a slang nickname for a doctor, and a medical man is an old-fashioned term for a physician.

clue.text: Take commercial: a blast from the past?

parts.note: 'take X' introduces an example, as e.g. (for example) does
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: Instructions to go with an advert, and a hint that it is a piece of nostalgia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' looks like a verb of action but stands for e.g., as in 'take, for example, ...'.
explanation.definitionFit: Egad is an archaic mild oath, so it is an exclamation (a blast) from earlier times.

clue.text: Assimilate 17 5 a 18 25!

parts.note: the cross-references read 'like many a true word', and the proverb says many a true word is spoken in jest

explanation.surface: An exclamatory instruction to take in a string of cross-referenced answers.
explanation.walkthrough: Substitute the answers to 17, 5, 18 and 25 to get 'like many a true word'; the proverb finishes 'is spoken in jest', and IN JEST said out loud is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingest is to take in and absorb food, and assimilate is a synonym for absorbing.

clue.text: Endlessly striving for better pain relief

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: aspiring means striving to achieve more

explanation.surface: Someone constantly seeking a better painkiller.
explanation.walkthrough: ASPIRING loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirin is a common analgesic drug taken to relieve pain.

clue.text: I'll be collecting unloaded auction lots

indicators.note: to collect something is to gather it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: 'Well, I'll be!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, the word keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of auction

explanation.surface: An auctioneer saying they will gather up lots that failed to sell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll be' reads as the start of a promise, but it is a surprised exclamation, the same as 'My!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lots used as a quantity word means a large number, as many does.

clue.text: With numbers short, 3 sandwiches = a picnic!

indicators.note: a sandwich holds its filling between two slices, so one piece is placed between others

parts.note: Nos is the short form of numbers
W is an abbreviation for with
3 down is INGEST, and to ingest is to eat

explanation.surface: A cheerful sum: with fewer people, the sandwich supply makes a picnic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like the picnic food but is the instruction to put one piece between the other two; 3 refers to the answer at 3 down.
explanation.definitionFit: 'It's no picnic' means it is hard, so a picnic is something easy, which is what the idiom no sweat says.

clue.text: Who's bringing the staff a nutmeg tree?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the official who carries the ceremonial staff, the mace, in a procession
second meaning, whimsical: the nutmeg tree produces the spice mace, so it bears mace

explanation.surface: Asking who will bring the employees a nutmeg tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like employees but is a rod of office; mace is also the spice made from the husk of the nutmeg.
explanation.definitionFit: A mace-bearer is the ceremonial official carrying a mace, the staff of authority, before a dignitary.

clue.text: Saw the Grand Master post each hour

indicators.note: post means after, so the first group of words is placed after the second

parts.note: 'a pop' means each, as in five pounds a pop
H is the abbreviation for hour
taken as written
GM is the chess title Grand Master

explanation.surface: Someone saw the chess Grand Master posting on social media every hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a past-tense verb but is a noun, an old saying; 'post' is Latin for after, not a social-media update.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a traditional saying or maxim, which is what an apophthegm is.

clue.text: Is this buzzer now loud?

parts.note: what is so now is set back in time, to its past tense
something loud now was earlier quiet, and p (piano) is the musical mark for quiet

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a buzzing insect or alarm has got louder.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'if it is now loud, it was p', i.e. was piano (soft) before; the answer splits 3,1 that way. 'This buzzer' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A buzzer is any insect that buzzes, and this striped stinging insect is a classic example.

clue.text: Wheels away rubbish bags

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car
'Away!' and 'Go!' are both orders to leave
pants is British slang for rubbish or nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone wheels the rubbish bags out to the bins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' looks like refuse sacks but is old slang for trousers; in Britain 'pants' also means underpants and, informally, rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Bags is a dated British term for loose trousers, and cargo pants are a kind of trousers.

clue.text: Come to evaluate trophy for auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the words are rendered as a hearer would catch them

parts.note: to weigh something up is to evaluate it, and a cup is a sporting trophy

explanation.surface: An instruction to come and value a trophy for the accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests an accountant but here means a listener: 'weigh cup' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to after fainting is to regain consciousness, which is what waking up means.

clue.text: Old boy given time security guards dock

indicators.note: to guard something is to surround and protect it, so one piece encloses the others

parts.note: bail is money given as security for a released prisoner
OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A former pupil is given a prison sentence and kept under guard in the court dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dock' looks like the courtroom enclosure but is a verb: to cut an animal's tail short.
explanation.definitionFit: To bobtail an animal is to cut its tail short, which is exactly what docking means.

clue.text: Flipping shrew let on about dress material

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the turned letters go around another word
flipping something over turns it the other way round

parts.note: to let on is to reveal a secret, to blab
a rig is an outfit of clothes
a shrew is a scolding woman, a nag

explanation.surface: An irritable woman reveals something about a dress fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild curse on the shrew but is the reversal signal; 'dress material' splits into wordplay and definition. Balbriggan is named after a town north of Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: Balbriggan is a knitted cotton fabric used for underwear and hosiery, so it is a material.

clue.text: Man on board so ill takes small dose of aperient salt

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so these words go within another

parts.note: bad means ill, as in feeling bad
the first letter of aperient, a small amount of it
the king is a piece (man) on a chessboard
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor feeling so seasick that he swallows a little laxative salt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man on board' suggests a ship's crewman but means a chess piece. BAD plus A holds KING SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, a chemical salt used in cooking and as an antacid.

clue.text: Cloth product's trade name

parts.note: a line is a trade or business, and also a range of products
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A fabric product's brand or trade name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trade name' looks like a single phrase, a brand, but splits into a line of business and an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Linen is a fabric woven from flax fibres, so it is a kind of cloth.

clue.text: He leaves the new rep without a function

indicators.note: when something leaves it is taken away, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: the letters removed from the following word
the word with its last two letters dropped

indicators.note: without can mean outside, so one word goes around another

parts.note: a sales rep is an agent
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A man leaves the new representative without any job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without a function' sounds like being unemployed, but 'without' means outside and 'a function' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangent is a trigonometric function, the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent one.

clue.text: A few present resistance further north …

indicators.note: in a down answer north is upward, so the letter is reinserted higher up

parts.note: to be there is to be present
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A handful of people present, with opposition moving further north, as in a news report.
explanation.walkthrough: In THERE the R moves up one place, which in a down entry means towards the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Three is a small number, so it can stand for a few things.

clue.text: Dark radio piece

indicators.note: on the radio words are heard rather than seen, so this is how they sound

parts.note: a knight is a piece in chess

explanation.surface: A gloomy item of radio programming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' suggests a radio feature but is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark as a noun means nightfall or night-time, as in 'after dark'.

clue.text: Dig, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning, informal: to dig something is to enjoy it
second meaning: the hedging filler, as in 'it'll take, ..., an hour'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dig, perhaps' looks like a gardening suggestion; both words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Dig is slang for be fond of, and the casual filler word hedges a statement, much as maybe does.

clue.text: Getting this right would make the Tories understand

definitions.text: Getting this right would make the Tories understand

parts.words: Getting this right would make the Tories understand
parts.note: surface reading: correcting something would bring the Conservative Party round
setter's reading: put the answer on the right of CONS (the Tories) and you get a word for understand; it also means right

explanation.surface: Fixing this would finally get the Conservatives to understand.
explanation.walkthrough: Cons is short for Conservatives (Tories); CONS followed by the answer spells CONSTRUE, to understand. The answer also means right, correct.
explanation.definitionFit: True and right both describe something correct or accurate.

clue.text: Person with a kit for repairing pipe

definitions.text: Person with a kit for repairing
definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who sews, using a sewing kit for mending
second meaning: a drain carrying waste water

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a plumber fixing a pipe; the word is read once as 'sew-er' and once as a drain.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewer is both one who sews (mends with needle and thread) and an underground drainage conduit.

clue.text: … as news got around a city

indicators.note: news that gets around spreads in every direction, so the letters are scattered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing 15: the news spread around a city.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to the previous clue but adds nothing to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Swansea is a coastal city in south Wales.

clue.text: Fanatic spoke for boxing clubs

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a spoke is a radial, a line running out from a hub
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: An extremist spoke in favour of boxing clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoke' looks like the past of speak but is a wheel's rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A radical is a person with extreme views, an extremist, which is what fanatic means.

clue.text: Badly in need of a holiday briefing

definitions.text: Badly in need of a holiday
definitions.meaning: first meaning: tired and worn out
second meaning: a summary of the main points

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an overworked staffer; the hyphenated form and the noun are separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Run-down describes exhaustion from overwork, and a rundown is a quick summary given as a briefing.

clue.text: It picks up sound when edge is taken, caught behind

indicators.note: taking the edges away means the outermost letters are removed

parts.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it
the rump is the behind, the backside

explanation.surface: Cricket commentary: the batsman edges the ball and is caught by the wicketkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught behind' is cricket's dismissal by the wicketkeeper, but here it is two words, HEARD and RUMP, whose outer letters are trimmed off.
explanation.definitionFit: The eardrum is the membrane that vibrates with sound waves and passes them to the inner ear.

clue.text: Erase marks from ruler?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, whimsical: to ... something, to remove its spots

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' looks like the measuring stick with marks on it; the answer read as DE-SPOT is a made-up verb, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is a tyrant holding absolute power, a ruler answerable to nobody.

clue.text: Stove's missing a supply pipe? I'll come out

definitions.text: Stove's missing a supply pipe? I'll come out

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so the named letter is dropped

parts.note: an Aga is a British range cooker, plus the 's

indicators.note: to come out of something is to leave it, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a main is a principal supply pipe for gas or water

explanation.surface: A customer reports a cooker problem, and the engineer promises a visit.
explanation.walkthrough: AGA'S loses an A and MAIN loses its I. The whole clue is the exchange with the engineer, who says 'I'll come out'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasman is an engineer from the gas company who visits homes to fix appliances and supply lines.

clue.text: A limit to well-founded rumour

parts.note: the opening letter of well-founded is one of its limits
'a limit' means one end or the other, so the two ends are offered as alternatives
the closing letter of well-founded is its other limit

explanation.surface: A curb on rumours that do have a basis in fact.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'W or D': a limit of well-founded is one end or the other, W or D.
explanation.definitionFit: Word can mean news or report, as in 'word has it', which is a rumour going around.

clue.text: Woman named herein

indicators.note: herein means inside these words, so the answer is sitting in the clue

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A woman whose name appears within this text.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the woman is named in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna is a common woman's first name.

clue.text: Deal one makes put an end to hunger

parts.note: to scotch a rumour or plan is to put an end to it
to pine for something is to long, or hunger, for it

explanation.surface: A deal that one person makes to end famine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' is not a bargain but the softwood timber of pine or fir.
explanation.definitionFit: Deal is pine or fir timber, and this conifer is a major source of it.

clue.text: A tragic heroine, I died in Carmen?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: car men are the AA, the Automobile Association, Britain's breakdown service
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: Asking whether a tragic heroine dies in Bizet's opera Carmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carmen' looks like Bizet's opera but splits into car men, Britain's AA breakdown patrol.
explanation.definitionFit: Aida is the title heroine of Verdi's opera, who dies entombed with her lover Radames.

clue.text: Departing founders of band call it what? Yadda Yadda Yadda

indicators.note: the founders are the first letters, and they depart, so each word loses its initial

parts.note: the four words taken as written

explanation.surface: Founding band members leave, and someone wonders what to call the group now; the reply is a shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: Each of the four words loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'And all that' and 'yadda yadda yadda' are both dismissive tags meaning 'and so on'.
